title: When Self-Service Becomes Self-Defence
summary: When self-service transfers labour, risk and accountability to customers, efficiency becomes fragile and the customer is left to defend themselves.
body_text: Yesterday, I flew home from Málaga with Ryanair. I was travelling with an oversized item: a child’s car seat. That put me outside the airline’s standard check-in process, although hardly into an unpredictable edge case. Ryanair carries millions of families. Car seats, pushchairs and oversized baggage are part of the everyday reality of running an airline. Yet the process felt as though it had been designed without any real thought. Checking in required a phone. The airport used dynamic QR codes. To deal with the car seat, I first had to find and flag down an assistant. The assistant then produced another QR code - not from a piece of airport equipment or an official check-in system, but apparently from WhatsApp on their phone - which I had to scan with mine. Consider how many things had to work for that interaction to succeed. My phone had to be charged, connected and in my hand. The right assistant had to be visible and available. I had to understand that there was a separate process for the car seat, despite there being little obvious guidance. Their phone had to be working. The QR code had to load. My camera had to recognise it. And we both had to complete this improvised digital handshake while surrounded by luggage, children, queues and the low-level anxiety that accompanies almost every airport departure. This may have reduced the amount of equipment or staffing Ryanair needed to provide. It did not feel efficient to me. More importantly, it did not look particularly efficient for the airport staff either. The process had not eliminated work. It had redistributed it. Some had been transferred to the passenger. Some remained with the assistant, who now had to be found and interrupted. Some had been turned into uncertainty, delay and repeated attempts. What appeared efficient from the centre became fragmented and fragile at the point of use. That is the curious thing about badly designed self-service. It asks the customer to become the employee, troubleshooter and quality-control department - then treats the customer as the problem when the process fails. Self-service becomes self-defence. Customers do not always have a meaningful choice The self-service check-in process at Málaga Airport It would be easy to dismiss this as a complaint about a budget airline. Ryanair is inexpensive. Its business model is built around operational efficiency. Everyone knows it is not selling luxury. But that misses the point. I was not looking for champagne, a red carpet or somebody to carry my bags. I wanted a clear, reliable process for checking in an item that families take onto flights every day. Nor was I standing in an ordinary competitive marketplace at that moment. Several airlines might fly between Spain and the UK. But once I had booked a particular journey, arrived at Málaga Airport and needed to get home at a particular time, the theoretical existence of another airline was largely irrelevant. Ryanair had what we might call a situational monopoly . It controlled the service I needed at the moment I needed it. Walking away was not a meaningful option. This is what makes some transactions different from ordinary purchases. Sometimes we choose a product because we want it. Sometimes we enter a service because circumstances compel us to complete it. We have to catch the flight. Submit the mortgage application. Make an insurance claim. Restore access to a frozen bank account. Prove our identity. Attend the hospital appointment. Fix the broadband connection. Resolve the fraudulent payment. Complete the visa process. Cancel the contract. These are distressed purchases or, more broadly, high-stakes service moments. The customer may have chosen the provider months or years earlier. They may theoretically be able to choose another one in the future. But inside the moment itself, they have little agency. They need the process to work, and the cost of failure belongs overwhelmingly to them. That imbalance matters because it can disguise poor service remarkably well. Customers still complete the journey. The transaction still converts. The flight remains full. The test gets booked. The form is eventually submitted. From the organisation’s point of view, the process appears successful. But completion is not the same as satisfaction. When customers cannot walk away, completion may not even be evidence that the service worked. It may simply reveal how much difficulty they were willing - or forced - to endure. We saw the other side of this with ExpressTest Our work with ExpressTest took place in a very different context, but it involved the same underlying service-design problem. During the pandemic, international travel was governed by testing requirements that changed frequently and differed between countries. For many journeys, passengers were required to obtain a valid negative Covid test within a specified window. UK government guidance directed travellers who needed tests towards private providers that met the relevant minimum standards. Testing was not an optional enhancement to the journey. It could determine whether the journey happened at all. [1] Our client became one of three solution providers operating in that space. At first glance, the proposition appeared simple: book a test, take the test and receive a result. But nobody was really buying a medical procedure. They were buying certainty that they could travel. Even that does not capture the whole emotional context, however. The test did not merely present an administrative risk. It presented a health risk. Customers were worried that their certificate might not arrive in time. They were worried that they had booked the wrong type of test. They were worried that they had misunderstood the entry requirements. They were worried about losing the money they had spent on flights, accommodation or family events. And, beneath all of this, they were worried that they might actually have Covid. A positive result did not simply mean a failed transaction. It could mean illness, isolation and possible transmission to someone they loved. It might mean being unable to attend a wedding, see a relative, return home or take a long-delayed holiday. During the most uncertain periods of the pandemic, it could provoke genuine fear about what would happen next. Research confirms that this was not a marginal emotional response. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis found high levels of Covid-related fear and anxiety across different populations, while a later review connected fear of Covid with anxiety, depression, stress, sleep problems and poorer mental wellbeing. [2, 3] This was therefore a service with two possible sources of distress: Will the process allow me to travel? What will the result tell me about my health? The customer needed logistical certainty while approaching an outcome that was inherently uncertain. That distinction shaped the challenge. We could not promise everyone the result they wanted. No honest service could. But we could design the experience so that people understood what would happen, what was required from them, where they were in the process and when they would hear from us. We could absorb as much procedural uncertainty as possible, because the customer was already carrying enough emotional uncertainty of their own. That, to me, is one of the most useful definitions of good service design: Good service design absorbs complexity on behalf of the customer. Bad service design exposes the customer to the organisation’s complexity and asks them to manage it. The problem is not self-service I am not against self-service. Good self-service can be faster, calmer and more convenient than waiting for an employee. I would rather check in online than queue at a desk. I would rather track a delivery than phone a call centre. I would rather make a simple change myself than explain it to three different people. The academic literature has recognised these benefits for decades. Self-service technologies can give customers more control, improve access and reduce waiting. But research also shows that satisfaction depends heavily on whether the technology actually solves the customer’s problem. One of the foundational studies in this field, published by Matthew Meuter, found that both the success of the technology and the customer’s ability to recover from a failure are central to the experience. [4] That is the crucial distinction. Self-service is valuable when it gives the customer agency. It becomes destructive when it merely transfers labour, risk and accountability to them. Researchers have described this transferred effort as “consumptive labour” or “shadow work”: unpaid work once performed by employees that is now performed by customers. [5] There is nothing automatically wrong with that exchange. I am happy to scan my own boarding pass if doing so saves time. I am happy to assemble a simple piece of furniture if that lowers its cost. I am happy to manage my account online if I gain speed and control in return. The problem begins when the value flows in only one direction. The organisation saves money, while I inherit another password, device dependency, unexplained error message or recovery process. The service has been optimised for the organisation’s cost-to-serve, but my own cost-to-be-served has been ignored. That cost is not limited to minutes. It includes attention, cognitive load, uncertainty and emotional effort. In a high-stakes situation, it also includes the risk of missing a flight, losing money, delaying medical treatment or being locked out of something essential. The happy path is not the service Many digital experiences are designed around a “happy path”: the cleanest sequence through which an ideal user completes a task. The passenger has the right document. The customer remembers their password. The applicant’s address history fits the form. The patient speaks the expected language. The traveller has a charged smartphone and reliable data. The luggage is a standard size. The test result is negative. Designing the happy path is useful, but it is not enough. The real quality of a service is revealed when something deviates from it. What happens when the passenger has a car seat? What happens when the customer cannot receive the verification code? What happens when the person has no smartphone, poor eyesight or limited dexterity? What happens when a result is inconclusive? What happens when the rules change between booking and travel? What happens when somebody is frightened? Exceptions are often discussed as if they were rare defects around the edge of the service. At sufficient scale, they are the service. A process used by millions of people will encounter dead batteries, forgotten passwords, accessibility needs, delayed messages, unusual names, disputed payments, distressed customers and luggage of every conceivable shape. None of these is surprising. The precise individual may be unpredictable. The existence of the exception is not. If the official journey cannot handle these circumstances, employees create unofficial ones. They use personal messages, handwritten notes, unofficial spreadsheets, screenshots and workarounds. That ingenuity may rescue the customer, but it also tells us something important: the service is relying on frontline improvisation to repair a design failure. This creates what systems thinker John Seddon calls failure demand : additional demand caused by an organisation failing to do something, or failing to do it correctly, the first time. The customer asks for help because the instructions were unclear. They call because the app did not explain the error. They approach a member of staff because the kiosk cannot handle the exception. Each contact appears as new work, but it is actually work generated by the original service. This is why badly designed self-service can create the illusion of efficiency. A task disappears from one departmental spreadsheet only to reappear somewhere less visible: in longer queues, repeated contacts, staff interruptions, customer anxiety and abandoned trust. Why conventional measures miss the damage The most dangerous feature of a distressed purchase is that many familiar business metrics become unreliable. A customer who successfully boards the flight counts as a completed transaction, even if they found the process bewildering. A traveller who receives a Covid certificate counts as a fulfilled order, even if they spent the previous 24 hours uncertain whether the result would arrive. A person who eventually recovers their bank account counts as a resolved case, even if it required four calls and caused days of anxiety. The organisation sees the outcome. The customer remembers the ordeal. Research into customer effort provides a useful corrective. Matthew Dixon, Karen Freeman and Nicholas Toman argued that reducing the work customers must do to solve a problem is a stronger route to loyalty than trying to manufacture elaborate “wow” moments. Their research found that difficult service interactions were especially likely to drive disloyalty. [6] I think this is particularly important in high-stakes services. “Delight” can sound frivolous when somebody is waiting for a medical result or trying to get home. The customer does not need theatre. They need clarity, competence and reassurance. In these moments, delight is often simply the absence of avoidable distress. It is seeing immediately which test you need. It is knowing that your booking has been received. It is understanding when the result will arrive. It is being told what happens if something goes wrong. It is finding a human being before you have exhausted every automated route. It is a fallback that feels like part of the service rather than an admission that the service has failed. Design for the emotional job, not only the functional task A service journey normally contains at least two layers. The first is functional: What is the customer trying to accomplish? The second is emotional: What are they trying to feel, or stop feeling, while accomplishing it? At ExpressTest, the functional job was obtaining a valid test result. The emotional job was achieving enough certainty to continue with an important journey while confronting the possibility of illness. At Málaga, the functional job was checking in a car seat. The emotional job was knowing that my family and our belongings were correctly processed and that we would be allowed to board the flight. A purely operational design sees the transaction. A genuinely customer-centred design sees what the transaction means. This is not a plea to make every interface sentimental. It is an argument for recognising that anxiety changes how people process information. Under pressure, customers have less patience for ambiguity and less cognitive capacity to decode unfamiliar instructions. Every unexplained step becomes evidence that something may be going wrong. The service should therefore communicate more clearly, not less, at moments of high uncertainty. This also connects with the peak-end rule , associated with the work of Daniel Kahneman and others. Research suggests that people’s memories of an experience are influenced disproportionately by its most emotionally intense moment and by how it ends. The principle has since been explored specifically in service settings. [7] For ExpressTest customers, opening the result was the emotional peak. The arrival of a valid certificate was the end of the service and the beginning of their journey. Those moments deserved disproportionate design attention. For an airline passenger, an unresolved problem at check-in may also become both the emotional peak and the final meaningful interaction with the airline before security. A fragile process at that point can colour the memory of the entire experience. Five questions every organisation should ask This issue extends far beyond airports and pandemic testing. Every organisation has moments in which the customer’s freedom, time or emotional bandwidth is constrained. Those moments deserve more scrutiny precisely because customers are less able to leave. I would start with five questions. 1. Where can our customers not realistically walk away? Look beyond legal monopolies. Find the situational ones. These may occur when a customer is locked into a contract, facing a deadline, dealing with an emergency or has already invested significant time and money. The question is not whether another provider exists. It is whether switching is a credible option in that particular moment. 2. What are customers really carrying? Map the emotional stakes as well as the transactional steps. Are customers confused, embarrassed, bereaved, frightened, angry or short of time? What happens if they make a mistake? What does the outcome mean beyond the immediate transaction? The same five-minute delay feels very different when ordering a T-shirt and when waiting to learn whether you can travel, or whether you have Covid. 3. Where have we transferred work without transferring value? List everything customers now do that an employee or system once did. Some of that work may be entirely reasonable. But what do customers receive in exchange: greater speed, control, convenience or lower cost? Where are they simply subsidising an internal efficiency programme with their own time and attention? 4. What happens outside the happy path? Do not ask only whether the main journey works. Test expired batteries, poor connectivity, accessibility needs, missing documents, unusual luggage, changed plans, inconclusive results and frightened people. Observe what frontline employees actually do, including the unofficial workarounds absent from the service blueprint. Those workarounds often contain the clearest evidence of what the formal service has failed to provide. 5. Are we measuring completion or confidence? Completion tells us whether the customer reached the end. Confidence tells us whether they knew what was happening, understood what was required and trusted the organisation to handle a problem. Both matter. Only one of them is normally visible on an operational dashboard. Useful measures might include repeated attempts, requests for clarification, avoidable contacts, time spent recovering from errors, intervention by frontline staff and the customer’s confidence at critical points, not just their eventual completion of the transaction. Efficiency and care are not opposites There is a tendency to frame this debate as a choice between commercial efficiency and customer care. That is too simplistic. A well-designed service can reduce both operational cost and customer effort. Clearer instructions can prevent calls. Better status updates can reduce uncertainty and repeated contact. Thoughtful exception handling can stop staff being interrupted. Accessible digital journeys can allow more customers to complete tasks independently. The goal is not to add a person to every interaction. It is to put human support where human judgement or reassurance is valuable, and ensure that digital systems do not generate the very demand they were introduced to remove. ExpressTest operated under extraordinary pressure: shifting regulation, significant volume, medical responsibility and customers with immovable travel deadlines. The answer was not to pretend that those constraints did not exist. It was to prevent as much of that complexity as possible from landing on the customer. That lesson applies anywhere a transaction carries consequences beyond the transaction itself. Customers may forget a slick animation or a clever piece of copy. They will remember whether the organisation made a frightening moment calmer. They will remember whether the process gave them confidence or made them feel foolish. They will remember whether someone took responsibility when the system stopped working. And they will remember being treated as a human being rather than as unpaid infrastructure. Self-service should extend our agency. It should make ordinary things easier and give us more control over our time. When it instead forces us to locate the right employee, obtain an unofficial QR code, diagnose the organisation’s process and protect ourselves against its failure, it has crossed a line. It is no longer self-service. It is self-defence. References UK Government, Private providers of coronavirus testing . Luo et al., Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Fear of COVID-19 . Şimşir et al., Fear of COVID-19 and its association with mental health-related factors . Meuter et al., Self-Service Technologies: Understanding Customer Satisfaction with Technology-Based Service Encounters . Koeber, Wright and Dingler, Self-Service in the Labor Process . Dixon, Freeman and Toman, Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers . Oxford Academic, The peak-end rule . Back to all posts

title: New America Acquisition I Corp. Announces Leadership Transition; Kyle Wool Appointed Chief Executive Officer
summary: Dominari Securities is dedicated to helping clients preserve, grow and create new wealth by providing a full range investment advisory and wealth planning services.
body_text: Chairman Kyle Wool, a veteran Wall Street executive, to lead the Company's pursuit of its anticipated initial business combination phase New York, New York, Aug. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- New America Acquisition I Corp. (NYSE: NWAX) (the "Company") today announced that Kevin McGurn has resigned as Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board of Directors of the Company, effective August 5, 2026, and that the Board of Directors has appointed Kyle Wool, the Company's Chairman of the Board, as Chief Executive Officer, effective as of the same date. Mr. Wool will continue to serve as Chairman of the Board. Mr. McGurn's resignation was voluntary and was not the result of any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to the Company's operations, policies or practices. The Company completed its initial public offering of 34,500,000 units at $10.00 per unit in December 2025, including the full exercise of the underwriters' over-allotment option, and continues to pursue its initial business combination targeting established U.S.-based companies across industrial automation, data and AI infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and the modernization of U.S. energy and power systems. "Leading New America from its founding through one of the most successful SPAC IPOs of 2025 has been a privilege, and I am proud of the platform and the team we have built," said Mr. McGurn. "Kyle is a proven capital markets leader with deep relationships across Wall Street and a long record of building businesses and delivering for investors. He knows this Company, he believes in its mission, and I can think of no one better positioned to carry it forward. I have complete confidence in Kyle and the Board, and I look forward to the Company completing an outstanding business combination." "On behalf of the Board, I want to thank Kevin for his leadership and for the strong foundation he built," said Mr. Wool. "Looking ahead, I am excited to complete a business combination with a great company that advances American industry and innovation and improves value for Americans. With the capital raised in our offering and a deep pipeline of opportunities across the sectors we know best, New America has the team, the resources and the mandate to deliver on that mission." Kyle Wool brings more than two decades of experience across financial services and capital markets. He has served as president of Dominari Holdings Inc. (Nasdaq: DOMH) since December 2023 and chief executive officer of Dominari Securities LLC since May 2023. Earlier in his career, Wool was an executive director at Morgan Stanley, advising clients on investment strategy and capital allocation. He also held senior roles at Oppenheimer and Co., including serving as managing director of the Professional Investors Group for Oppenheimer Asia Ltd. Wool holds a degree from the State University of New York at Binghamton. About New America Acquisition I Corp New America Acquisition I Corp is a blank-check company formed for the purpose of effecting a merger, capital stock exchange, asset acquisition, stock purchase, reorganization, or similar business combination with one or more businesses. The Company intends to target established U.S.-based companies that contribute to industrial capacity, technological innovation, and economic resilience, with a focus on automation, advanced manufacturing, infrastructure and energy systems. title: Meet the DV Fraud Lab’s New “Special Agents”
summary: As bad actors use agentic AI to scale their ad fraud schemes faster than ever, the DV Fraud Lab is using the same technology to protect our advertisers.
body_text: It has been a hot ad fraud summer at DV. In July alone, the DV Fraud Lab detected 34% more bot scheme variants than we did last July. We flagged nearly two billion requests from the sophisticated ViperBot scheme, which spoofs premium video inventory on mobile and CTV devices. And we identified a significant spike in an adware scheme targeting Android devices . The DV Fraud Lab attributes these dramatic surges in activity to agentic AI, which is accelerating the pace at which fraud schemes scale, spike and multiply. But DV’s fraud fighters are moving just as quickly to protect our advertiser customers’ campaigns. Our secret weapon? Also agentic AI. DV is using our massive proprietary data and fraud expertise to build AI skills that investigate along with us, like research buddies that never get tired. Built by DV’s Fraud Analytics Engineering Group in collaboration with the Fraud Research Engineering Team, the agents learn from human domain experts to dynamically collect and analyze evidence and prioritize leads at superhuman speed. In a matter of hours, they can proceed from fraud detection to evidence-gathering to mitigation, a process that might take a human a couple of days . These AI game-changers help the Fraud Lab mitigate dozens of schemes, which together account for hundreds of millions of impressions, every day. DV’s AI Agents in Action To demonstrate, here’s how a DV mobile fraud agent helped us quickly respond to a fraudulent mobile app scheme, “Puppet Smash.” To determine whether the app was fraudulent, a human investigator would first need to analyze its underlying code and configuration to spot red flags that signal malicious intent. The work is painstaking and requires reasoning and judgment, not just pattern-matching. The Fraud Lab’s AI agent does much of this analysis for us. It automatically detects evasion methods in the app’s code and circumvents them to reveal the app’s true nature. Then it tests the app and documents its behavior with a screenshot and a report. AI agents also helped DV uncover the adware scheme we’ve named AfterCall. In an AfterCall attack, a malicious app dodges built-in platform safeguards, tricks a smartphone user into granting overlay permissions, then begins firing ads every time the user ends a phone call. Our agents have helped us swiftly respond to this proliferating threat. DV’s Agentic Fraud Lab Has You Covered As of early 2026, AI agents, tools, skills and workflows are fully integrated into DV Fraud Lab operations as part of DV Neura™, the cognitive engine that powers our platform. DV has shut down thousands of web, in-app and streaming/CTV fraud properties and schemes over the past few years. By providing enhanced fraud detection coverage that keeps pace with the growth in fraud attempts, our AI agents help keep the industry, and your ad dollars, safe. Next Steps Contact a DV representative.

title: Annexon Reports First U.S. and European Patient Cohort of GBS FORWARD Study Demonstrated Rapid, Positive Clinical Responses in All Tanruprubart Treated Patients Within One Week
summary: Early Outcomes Reinforce the Consistency and Reproducibility of Tanruprubart Treatment Effect Previously Demonstrated in Phase 3 and Real-World Evidence Studies Potential to Become the First Approved Targeted Therapy to Treat GBS Worldwide, Addressing the Significant Unmet Need and Over $20
body_text: PDF Version Early Outcomes Reinforce the Consistency and Reproducibility of Tanruprubart Treatment Effect Previously Demonstrated in Phase 3 and Real-World Evidence Studies Potential to Become the First Approved Targeted Therapy to Treat GBS Worldwide, Addressing the Significant Unmet Need and Over $20 Billion Estimated Annual U.S. Healthcare Burden FORWARD Data to Support BLA Submission Targeted for Q4 2026; Tanruprubart Currently Under Review by the EMA BRISBANE, Calif., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Annexon, Inc. (Nasdaq: ANNX), a biopharmaceutical company advancing the next generation platform of targeted immunotherapies for multiple neuroinflammatory diseases that impact nearly 10 million people worldwide, today announced early improvement in strength and clinically meaningful reduction in disability shown with tanruprubart in the first ten U.S. and European patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) from its ongoing, open-label FORWARD study. GBS is a life-threatening neuroinflammatory disease that can cause rapid and severe weakness or complete paralysis, often requiring intensive care and mechanical ventilation. It is the leading cause of acute neuromuscular paralysis with approximately 22,000 patients affected annually across the U.S. and Europe, and an estimated >$20 billion annual healthcare burden in the U.S . alone. In the 110 years since GBS was described, there have been no approved targeted therapies that rapidly and meaningfully impact the disease. Current standard-of-care intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg), which is not FDA-approved, provides incomplete benefit for many patients. Indeed, despite standard of care use, mortality rates associated with GBS are up to 10%1 generally, and nearly 25% in GBS patients over the age of 65 within one year of hospitalization. Moreover, many IVIg-treated patients frequently progress during or shortly after treatment, resulting in ventilatory support in one of four patients, prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) stays, inability to walk unassisted for months to years, and continued physical and psychological limitations, pain and severe fatigue. Notably, initial cohort FORWARD data (n=10) showed clinically meaningful and rapid improvement in strength and reduced disability within days of a single infusion of 30 mg/kg tanruprubart. Outcomes include: All patients treated in the study showed rapid, clinically meaningful improvement in muscle strength within four days. Four patients who were bedbound early in the course of their disease walked with or without assistance between day two and eight. The one patient who required ventilation early in the course of disease came off the ventilator within four days. Five other patients all showed marked gains in function within 48 hours. Tanruprubart was generally well-tolerated, with most common adverse events related to GBS or complications with the disease consistent with Phase 3 results. Initial cohort included both male and female patients, ranging in age from 12 to 78 years old, and covered the spectrum of disease from moderate to severe. Outcomes of the FORWARD trial are consistent with outcomes demonstrated in the GBS Phase 3 study where approximately 90% of patients demonstrated rapid, clinically meaningful improvement by day 8 of treatment. “The early results from the FORWARD study are some of the most encouraging we have seen in GBS research and reinforce the potential of tanruprubart as a transformative treatment,” said Rafid Mustafa, M.D., Associate Professor of Neurology and Vice Chair for Quality, Department of Neurology, Mayo Clinic. “We are optimistic about what this may mean for patients. Restoring strength and mobility is not simply a clinical milestone; it is a pathway back to independence, dignity, and everyday life.” Thomas Harbo, M.D., Ph.D., Professor of Neurology, Aarhus University, and Consultant Neurologist, Aarhus University Hospital in Denmark remarked, “The speed of responses with tanruprubart are striking. Patients who may have otherwise faced an uncertain road to recovery showed remarkable improvements in strength within days, translating into enhanced function and early mobilization. Thus far, the findings reinforce the potential of tanruprubart to stop the underlying disease process rather than just supporting patients through it.” Douglas Love, president and chief executive officer of Annexon added, “The early and marked improvements in this initial data from FORWARD are consistent with our Phase 3 and Real World Evidence findings. That consistency continues to strengthen the significant functional outcomes being achieved with our differentiated C1q-focused approach targeting neuroinflammation at its source. It also reflects our decade-long commitment to bringing disease-modifying treatments to help millions of people in need live their best lives.” Data from FORWARD will be presented at upcoming medical conferences and are expected to support consistent clinical benefit of tanruprubart across global patient populations to supplement Annexon's planned Biologics License Application (BLA) submission targeted for Q4 2026. The Marketing Authorisation Application (MAA) for tanruprubart is currently under review by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). 1 Doets AY, Verboon C, van den Berg B, et al. Regional variation of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Brain. 2018;141(10):2866-2877. About the FORWARD Study FORWARD is designed to give Western physicians and patients experience with tanruprubart, including in pediatric patients, and to support a broad intended label. The ongoing, open-label study is evaluating PK, PD, early impact on function and biomarkers, and safety of tanruprubart in adult and pediatric patients with GBS in the U.S. and Europe. About Tanruprubart Annexon’s lead investigational therapy, tanruprubart, is a first-in-class targeted and rapid-acting agent designed to reduce inflammation and nerve damage by stopping C1q activity in the peripheral and central nervous systems. Tanruprubart is administered intravenously and has been observed to act almost immediately in blocking C1q function. The aim of an effective treatment in GBS is to rapidly stop the neuroinflammatory damage on nerve cells, allowing patients to recover sooner, regain independence and return to pre-illness activities. Tanruprubart has received both Fast Track and Orphan Drug designations from the FDA as well as orphan drug designation from the EMA for the treatment of GBS. About Guillain-Barré Syndrome GBS is a rare neuromuscular emergency resulting from an acute autoantibody and classical complement-mediated attack on peripheral nerves that generally occurs post-infection in otherwise healthy persons. It is an acute, rapidly progressive disease with a narrow timeframe for therapeutic intervention. GBS results in the hospitalization of more than 22,000 people annually in the U.S. and Europe. The peripheral nerve damage progresses rapidly, causing acute neuromuscular paralysis that can lead to significant morbidity, disability and mortality. Currently, there are no approved treatments for GBS in the U.S. The long-term disease burden associated with GBS has led to a multi-billion-dollar annual economic cost to the U.S. healthcare system alone. More information about the impact of GBS is available at MoveGBSForward.com. About Annexon Annexon Biosciences (Nasdaq: ANNX) is advancing the next generation platform of targeted immunotherapies for nearly 10 million people worldwide living with serious neuroinflammatory diseases. Our founding scientific approach focuses on C1q, the initiating molecule of a potent inflammatory pathway that when misdirected can lead to tissue damage and loss of function in a host of diseases. Our targeted therapies are designed to stop classical complement-driven neuroinflammation at its source to provide meaningful functional benefit and alter the course of disease. Annexon’s mission is to deliver game-changing therapies to patients so that they can live their best lives. To learn more visit annexonbio.com . title: Rocket Lab Unveils GHOST Deployable Launch System to Enable Responsive Space Missions Worldwide
summary: LONG BEACH, Calif., Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocket Lab Corporation (Nasdaq: RKLB), a global leader in launch services and space systems today unveiled GHOST: a new globally-deployable containerized launch system to enable suborbital and orbital launches from anywhere in the world.
body_text: Rocket Lab Unveils GHOST Deployable Launch System to Enable Responsive Space Missions Worldwide August 10, 2026 PDF Version LONG BEACH, Calif., Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocket Lab Corporation (Nasdaq: RKLB), a global leader in launch services and space systems today unveiled GHOST: a new globally-deployable containerized launch system to enable suborbital and orbital launches from anywhere in the world. The GHOST (Global Hypersonic & Orbital Spaceport Technology) system transforms Rocket Lab’s Electron and HASTE rockets into a launch-anywhere, launch-anytime capability for multi-launch flight campaigns and critical national security missions. Packaged entirely within standard shipping containers, GHOST deploys complete rockets, launch infrastructure, ground support, and range control systems anywhere in the world. GHOST’s first location – named Rocket Lab Launch Complex 4 – will be at the Pacific Spaceport Complex at Kodiak, Alaska, with two pads to be established for high-frequency launch campaigns. The two pads will complement Rocket Lab’s existing suborbital and orbital launch sites at Launch Complex 1 in New Zealand, and Launch Complex 2 and Launch Complex 3 in Virginia, bringing the total number of pads operated by Rocket Lab to six across two hemispheres. The system is set to make its operational debut with a suborbital launch from Alaska in 2027. Because both Electron and HASTE use the same ground infrastructure, GHOST delivers a dual-launch capability across new locations, allowing Rocket Lab to expand the mission profiles of both vehicles and meet increasing international demand for orbital and suborbital sovereign launch capability. GHOST’s modular and small footprint is purpose-built to support responsive launch needs and time-critical national security missions, enabling rapid site activation and simultaneous launch possibilities. Sir Peter Beck, founder and CEO of Rocket Lab, says: “We’ve been leading the field in small launch for missile defense and national security for years. Our reliability, repeatability, and affordability sets us apart from everybody else, and creating GHOST is about packaging that up into a deployable system that can serve the world’s most important programs from wherever those missions need. Whether it’s for missile defense and deterrence, or opening up more trajectories, orbital missions, and sovereign launch capabilities in allied nations, GHOST is the answer to launching anywhere, anytime, and without compromise.” Rocket Lab Media Contact Murielle Baker media@rocketlabusa.com About Rocket Lab Rocket Lab (Nasdaq: RKLB) is an end-to-end space company delivering rockets, satellites, and spacecraft components for commercial, government, and defense missions. Driven by its industry-leading small-lift rockets Electron and HASTE and its upcoming reusable Neutron medium-lift rocket, Rocket Lab delivers reliable and responsive launch for the world’s most important missions from constellation deployment to missile defense. Rocket Lab’s satellites and components have powered more than 1,700 missions in Earth orbit, as well as deep-space exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Learn more at www.rocketlabcorp.com . title: PowerBank Acquires New York Solar Portfolio with US$32.5 Million Construction Value and US$13 Million in Expected U.S. Federal Tax Credits
summary: PowerBank Acquires New York Solar Portfolio with US$32.5 Million Construction Value and US$13 Million in Expected U.S. Federal Tax Credits
body_text: 13.9 MW of New York community solar projects expected to be construction-ready in 2026 and 2027 Toronto, Ontario, August 18, 2026 — PowerBank Corporation (Nasdaq: PBK) (Cboe CA: PBK) (FSE: 103) (“ PowerBank ” or the " Company "), a leader in independent energy development and asset ownership in North America, is pleased to announce that it has executed repurchase agreements for the Gainesville and Highway 28 projects (the “ Projects ”), located in New York state through its US subsidiary Abundant Solar Power Inc. The Highway 28 project is 6.9 megawatts and is expected to be construction ready in Q3 2026. It has secured its interconnection agreement, all major discretionary permits and has been approved for NYSERDA incentives under the NY-Sun program in the amount of US$893,445 and is expected to be eligible for a further approximately US$1,518,660 in NYSERDA incentives through the Inclusive Community Solar Adder program. The project is also expected to qualify for grants issued by the Catskills Watershed Corporation. As EPC contractor on the Highway 28 Project, Abundant Solar Power Inc. has commenced onsite prep work in advance of full construction mobilization. The Highway 28 Project is expected to remain eligible for the United States federal Investment Tax Credits for energy projects under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, as physical work began on the Project prior to the July 4, 2026 deadline and the physical work is expected to meet the requirements under the IRS Physical Work Test. The Project has a total construction value of approximately US$17 million and an expected ITC value of approximately US$8 million. The Highway 28 Project was acquired for a total purchase price of US$1,249,488, to be paid in milestone payments. The acquisition includes all project assets. The Gainesville project is 7 MW and is expected to be construction ready in 2027. It has secured its interconnection agreement and is currently in permitting. The project is expected to qualify for grants issued under NYSERDA’s NY-Sun program. The project company, which is owned by Abundant Solar Power Inc., is currently party to a lawsuit as Petitioner, known as Article 78 Index No. 9002873 involving an appeal of the denial of Petitioner’s variance application. The Gainesville Project is expected to remain eligible for the United States federal Investment Tax Credits for energy projects under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, as physical work began on the Project prior to the July 4, 2026 deadline and the physical work is expected to meet the requirements under the IRS Physical Work Test. The Project has a total construction value of approximately US$15.5 million and an expected ITC value of approximately US$5 million. The Gainesville Project was acquired for a total purchase price of US$1,146,580, to be paid in milestone payments. The acquisition includes all project assets. Investment Tax Credits have been available for solar projects since 2006, providing a 30% tax credit for commercial solar installations that meet specific requirements, with opportunities for ITC bonus adders. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law on July 4, 2025, specifies that the Section 48E Investment Tax Credit for solar facilities will be phased out, and projects which have begun construction on or before July 4, 2026, will remain eligible for the tax credits. Once completed, the Projects will be operated as community solar projects. Community solar is a group of solar panels with access to the local electricity grid. Once the panels are turned on and generating electricity, clean energy from the site feeds into the local power grid. Depending on the size and number of panels the project has, dozens or even hundreds of renters and homeowners can save money from the electricity that is generated by the project. By subscribing to a project, a homeowner earns credits on their electric bill every month from their portion of the solar power that’s generated by the project, accessing the benefits of solar without installing panels on their home. This allows homeowners to realize a reduced cost per kW/hour from the power they consume versus standard utility rates. The Projects were previously sold to an investor as part of a larger transaction announced on January 6, 2025 and have now been reacquired as initially announced on April 13, 2026 . Dr. Richard Lu, PowerBank’s CEO, commented: "We are excited to be growing our independent power producer portfolio by reacquiring two distributed solar projects in New York State. These are projects we originated, developed and secured interconnection for, so we understand them thoroughly, and we know what it takes to bring them to commercial operation. The acquisition of these projects supports our continued shift toward asset ownership, which builds recurring revenue. As Highway 28 is in advanced stages of development, we are looking forward to full onsite mobilization in the coming months.” There are several risks associated with the development of the Projects. The development of any project is subject to required permits, the continued availability of third-party financing arrangements for the Company, the risks associated with the construction of a solar power project and the degradation of solar panels over time. In addition, governments may revise, reduce or eliminate incentives and policy support schemes for solar power projects, which could result in future projects no longer being economic. title: ADNOC Deploys SLB Technology Across its Rig Fleet Through AI-Enabled Operations Center
summary: Sovereign cloud deployment enables faster decisions, earlier risk detection and secure AI-powered operations at scale
body_text: Sovereign cloud deployment enables faster decisions, earlier risk detection and secure AI-powered operations at scale ADNOC has deployed its AI-enabled Real-Time Operations Center (RTOC) across its fleet of more than 120 onshore and offshore drilling rigs, enabled by SLB’s DrillOps™ intelligent well delivery and insights solutions. The platform brings live drilling data into a unified, real-time environment that helps ADNOC teams improve coordination, identify risks earlier and make faster, more informed decisions. Developed in the United Arab Emirates and hosted within ADNOC’s sovereign cloud environment, the RTOC keeps critical operational data and workflows in-country while providing a secure foundation for AI-enabled operations at scale. The platform gives business, asset and drilling teams greater visibility across the fleet while supporting ADNOC’s data security, operational resilience and long-term digital independence objectives. “DrillOps transforms real-time drilling data into operational intelligence that helps teams make faster, more informed decisions,” said Rakesh Jaggi, president, Digital, SLB. “Deployed within ADNOC’s sovereign cloud environment, the technology provides the scalable digital foundation for AI-enabled workflows across one of the industry’s largest rig fleets and supports the continued progression toward more autonomous operations.” According to ADNOC, the deployment reduces engineering effort by 30% to 40% and enables engineers to support two to three times more rigs while maintaining effective oversight. Analyses that previously required a full day can now be completed within minutes, while reporting cycles that once took several days can be completed within hours. The RTOC combines operational data, automated dashboards, advanced analytics and AI-driven insights to turn large volumes of drilling data into clear, actionable information. This helps engineers focus on execution while maintaining visibility across a large and complex rig fleet. ADNOC said the platform can also identify potential operational issues before they escalate, reduce incident response times by 4 to 12 hours and help avoid one to two days of rig downtime. The deployment advances ADNOC’s broader effort to apply AI at scale across its operations while demonstrating how SLB digital technology can help operators move from fragmented data and manual analysis toward more connected and intelligent drilling operations. By embedding AI-enabled insights directly into operational workflows, the platform supports improved performance, reduced operational risk and greater efficiency across upstream operations.

title: Leidos continues to strengthen U.S. Navy’s secure intelligence operations
body_text: RESTON, Va. (August 3, 2026) – Leidos (NYSE: LDOS) will continue modernizing the infrastructure underpinning secure naval intelligence systems worldwide through a recent contract worth up to $64.8 million from the Office of Naval Intelligence. The agreement, which is for a base year with four option years, advances work Leidos has performed since 2021 and will help improve operational reliability, secure information sharing and accelerate technology integration for the Hopper Global Communications Center (GCC). “Modern intelligence operations depend on digital infrastructure that performs securely and reliably across the globe,” said Chad Haferbier, senior vice president of Decision Advantage at Leidos. “We are helping the Office of Naval Intelligence modernize that foundation so trusted information reaches warfighters faster.” The Hopper GCC provides IT services that rapidly disseminate intelligence to decision makers in the Navy and across the Department of War. Its systems manage some of the military’s most highly controlled information. This work advances Leidos' NorthStar 2030 strategy by strengthening two of the company's core growth pillars, cyber and mission & digital solutions, while delivering secure, resilient capabilities in support of national security.
